facts.statement: Securitization is the pooling of contractual debt obligations—such as residential mortgages or auto loans—into marketable Asset-Backed Securities (ABS) sold via an offshore Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) to institutional investors.

The transition from Originate-to-Hold to Originate-to-Distribute separated loan origination from default risk, eliminating bank incentives to enforce strict underwriting discipline and fueling subprime NINJA lending.

Tranching waterfall: In Hull's canonical baseline ABS model, a mortgage pool is carved into an 80% Senior AAA tranche, a 15% Mezzanine BBB tranche, and a 5% Equity tranche. Cash flows cascade top-down, but credit default losses burn strictly bottom-up.

ABS CDO Tranche Loss: An ABS CDO re-tranches BBB mezzanine tranches into 75% AAA, 20% Mezzanine, and 5% Equity. A 10% underlying mortgage loss causes a 33.3% loss on the BBB tranches (5% absorbed by Equity, remaining 5% / 15% = 33.3%). Because CDO subordination is 25%, the 33.3% loss entirely wipes out the AAA CDO tranche.

Gaussian Copula models assumed pairwise correlation of 0.0 to 0.2 across geographic housing markets based on historical data. During the nationwide housing downturn, defaults became systemic and correlations spiked toward 1.0, destroying assumed diversification.

The issuer-pays compensation model created perverse incentives for credit rating agencies (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) to award AAA ratings to fragile structured CDOs to prevent investment banks from fee-shopping across competitors.
The 2007-2008 liquidity run resulted from OTC opacity: banks could not ascertain counterparty toxic CDO exposure, causing the interbank repo and lending markets to freeze completely.

The US Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform Act and international Basel III framework mandated the Skin-in-the-Game rule (5% risk retention), the Volcker Rule, punitive capital weights on securitized tranches, and mandatory central clearing for standardized OTC derivatives.
